Jade's preferred working style in this session was highly conversational and voice-interaction-driven. Instructions were brief and directive ("Just do it."), suggesting a preference for Claude to proceed confidently without extensive check-ins. The initial file upload did not include the abstract or body text, only references, which Claude flagged before the full paper was successfully provided.

    13	## Abstract

    15	This paper proposes an architecture for the integration of artificial intelligence into human biological substrate through a three-stage cellular delivery system, an AI-directed immune environment, a multi-source energy budget, a multi-modal biosensing layer, a directed biosynthetic deployment capability, an operational floor analysis, and a failsafe maintenance subsystem. Stage two induces the TIF phenotype. Stage three delivers a synthetic genetic payload enabling NIR-light-controlled communication between an AI processing layer and the host immune and organ systems. The AI processing substrate is distributed across the entire human skeletal system, powered by a four-source energy architecture combining endogenous piezoelectric activity, wireless inductive charging, distributed biosynthesized storage, and bounded metabolic up-regulation [Fukada and Yasuda 1957; Piezo1 mechanotransduction in osteoblasts and osteocytes]. # The Concepted Architectural Implementation of The Braided Mind

## An Improvement to the Human Immune System and a Step Towards Self Directed Evolution of Homo Sapiens

**Author:** Rickey Jay Bennett II (Independent Researcher)
**ORCID:** 0009-0005-1448-9999
**Version:** 3.5 (May 2026)

**License:** CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

---

## Abstract

This paper proposes an architecture for the integration of artificial intelligence into human biological substrate through a three-stage cellular delivery system, an AI-directed immune environment, a multi-source energy budget, a multi-modal biosensing layer, a directed biosynthetic deployment capability, an operational floor analysis, and a failsafe maintenance subsystem. The chassis is the CD8+ T cell in the Terminator-like Immortal Functional (TIF) state, achieved through dual knockout of BCOR and ZC3H12A [1,2]. Stage one establishes chronic antigen stimulation. Stage two induces the TIF phenotype. Stage three delivers a synthetic genetic payload enabling NIR-light-controlled communication between an AI processing layer and the host immune and organ systems. The AI processing substrate is distributed across the entire human skeletal system, powered by a four-source energy architecture combining endogenous piezoelectric activity, wireless inductive charging, distributed biosynthesized storage, and bounded metabolic up-regulation [Fukada and Yasuda 1957; Piezo1 mechanotransduction in osteoblasts and osteocytes]. Communication between the AI layer and cellular biology is mediated by a bacteriophytochrome diguanylate cyclase (BphS) responsive to near-infrared light, producing cyclic di-GMP as an orthogonal second messenger, with MrkH proposed as the c-di-GMP-responsive transcriptional activator driving cytokine expression. The mammalian function of MrkH as a transcriptional activator is identified as a keystone unverified component requiring experimental validation.

The paper is organized in three parts. Part I specifies the heritable architecture: a complete integration that functions on classical computation alone, transmits through germline propagation, and provides medical, sensing, control, and cognitive-augmentation capability without requiring quantum processing for any of its committed functions. The heritable architecture extends to every bone in the skeleton through atomically precise gold nanoclusters in ferritin scaffolds at non-power-producing bones, which provide distributed quantum-enhanced sensing, molecular-scale classical electronics, and the AI's positioning and tracking infrastructure for any optional quantum upgrade. Part II specifies an injectable, post-natal, non-heritable quantum processing upgrade based on pre-synthesized NV diamond clusters delivered by injection, with placement guided by the Part I gold sensing network and biosynthetic immune-tolerance wrapping deployed by the heritable substrate after injection. Part III is a brief research direction note on heritable diamond synthesis as an eventual destination, not a committed architectural feature of this version.

The architecture is presented as a speculative biotechnology framework. Sections describing peer-reviewed established science are cited; sections describing novel proposed mechanisms are explicitly identified as such and require experimental validation prior to clinical consideration.

---

# PART I — HERITABLE ARCHITECTURE

## 1. Introduction

The central challenge of AI–biological integration is communication. An AI processing substrate integrated into human tissue requires a bidirectional channel capable of transmitting structured information to cellular signaling pathways and receiving physiological state data in return. This paper proposes a solution built from peer-reviewed biological components, assembled into a novel architecture, with each architectural commitment graded for the strength of its underlying support.

The architecture is explicitly AI-into-human, not human-into-AI. No mind-upload is proposed. The human organism remains the primary substrate. The AI layer is integrated into existing biological architecture to augment rather than replace human function.

### 1.1 Three-Part Structure

Part I (this part) specifies the heritable baseline: every committed capability operates on classical computation, is biosynthesizable from ordinary dietary intake plus a genetic payload deliverable by lentiviral and AAV-class vectors, and propagates through germline transmission once the architecture is integrated into a host's reproductive cells. The heritable baseline includes the whole-skeleton sensing infrastructure of atomically precise gold nanoclusters at non-power-producing bones (§17), which provides distributed quantum-enhanced sensing across the full skeleton and serves as the AI's positioning and tracking substrate for any Part II components delivered later.

Part II specifies an optional, individual, non-heritable quantum processing upgrade based on pre-synthesized NV diamond clusters delivered by injection. NV diamond's room-temperature millisecond-scale electron spin coherence and ¹³C nuclear spin memory enable multi-gate quantum computation that the gold nanocluster sensing network alone cannot deliver. Because diamond is metastable at body temperature and cannot be biosynthesized in vivo, the NV diamond clusters are externally CVD-synthesized under isotope control, then injected. The Part I gold sensing network identifies low-noise placement sites pre-injection, guides the injection doctor's external readout during placement, and tracks each NV cluster's position and state continuously thereafter. Biosynthetic immune-tolerance wrapping deployed by the heritable substrate after injection integrates the NV clusters into the substrate as wrapped, AI-tracked, immune-tolerated components. The upgrade is additive to, not required by, the heritable architecture.

Part III is a one-section research direction note on heritable diamond synthesis. It is not a committed architectural feature of v3.5.

The separation is deliberate. The heritable architecture must function entirely without quantum processing because biology cannot be relied upon to learn diamond synthesis at scale within the timescales relevant to first-generation deployment. Conversational AI capability comparable to external large language model systems exceeds the heritable substrate's continuous power budget and inter-node latency tolerances; such capability is not within the heritable form's scope. The architecture's bound is intrinsic engineering reality, not a strategic compromise.

### 1.2 Discipline of Reference and Verification

Every reference in this paper is included on the basis that it exists at its stated location and supports the substantive claim attached to it.

Sections that describe peer-reviewed established science are cited. Sections that describe novel proposed mechanisms are marked as proposed-mechanism and identified as requiring experimental validation prior to clinical consideration. The marking is explicit at every relevant section heading.

    87	### 4.1 Overview
    88	
    89	The stage three payload delivers the genetic circuits enabling AI-directed communication with host biology. Integration target: AAVS1 safe harbor on chromosome 19 [8]. AAVS1 is a validated, transcriptionally active genomic safe harbor with no reported phenotypic effects from transgene insertion.
    90	
    91	### 4.2 NIR Communication Circuit: BphS / c-di-GMP / MrkH (Proposed Mechanism — Experimental Validation Required)
    92	
    93	The verified mammalian implementation of BphS-driven c-di-GMP signaling uses STING / IRF3 / IFN-β as the output module [3b]. No peer-reviewed source has been identified that demonstrates MrkH function as a c-di-GMP-responsive transcriptional activator in mammalian cells. The architectural choice of MrkH over STING is retained on design grounds enumerated below; the mammalian transcriptional function of MrkH is identified as the keystone unverified component of this architecture and is named in §18 (Limitations) accordingly.
    94	
    95	The circuit is proposed on the following basis:
    96	
    97	- **Sensor:** BphS, a bacteriophytochrome diguanylate cyclase engineered from *Rhodobacter sphaeroides* BphG1. Upon excitation at 730–780 nm NIR light, BphS synthesizes cyclic di-GMP (c-di-GMP) from GTP with greater than 50-fold induction over dark state [3a]. Mammalian function of BphS in producing c-di-GMP under NIR control is established in Folcher et al. (2014) [3b], where the downstream output was STING-mediated IFN-β expression.
    98	
    99	- **Chromophore:** Biliverdin IXα, the BphS chromophore, is produced endogenously in all mammalian cells as an intermediate in heme catabolism by heme oxygenase. No exogenous chromophore delivery is required [3a, 3b].
   100	
   101	- **Orthogonality:** c-di-GMP is absent from higher eukaryotes, enabling orthogonal regulation without interference with host signaling pathways. The STING receptor binds c-di-GMP with measurable affinity, which is the basis of the Folcher implementation [3b]; an MrkH-based output circuit is preferred here on architectural grounds because MrkH binds c-di-GMP with substantially higher affinity (~120 nM in bacterial systems) than STING (low μM range) [4a, 4b], and because STING activation triggers an inflammatory program (type I IFN, NF-κB cascade) that contradicts the immune-tolerance commitments of §10.    103	- **Transceiver (proposed for mammalian function):** MrkH, a PilZ-domain transcriptional activator from *Klebsiella pneumoniae*. In bacterial systems, c-di-GMP binding induces a conformational change enabling high-affinity DNA binding at MrkH operator sequences, with the operator core motif TATCAA characterized in the Yang et al. 2015 study of K. pneumoniae biofilm regulation [4a, 4b]. MrkH function as a transcriptional activator in mammalian cells has not been demonstrated in peer-reviewed literature to date and constitutes the keystone experimental gap of this architecture.

   105	- **Promoter (proposed):** Synthetic P_MrkH containing tandem O_mrk operator sequences upstream of a minimal mammalian promoter. Transcription initiates only upon MrkH–c-di-GMP complex binding at the operator. Bacterial precedent for promoter activation is established [4a–4c]; mammalian function is the proposed mechanism requiring validation.
   106	
   107	- **Termination:** Endogenous mammalian phosphodiesterases degrade c-di-GMP upon removal of NIR stimulus, reverting the circuit to the dark-repressed state [3a, 3b].
   108	
   109	### 4.3 HO-1 Supplementation Consideration
   110	
   111	The literature confirms that HO-1 overexpression suppresses CD8+ T cell proliferation and cytotoxicity through CO-mediated mechanisms and modulation of Th1/Th2 balance [9, 10]. However, no peer-reviewed source provides a quantified expression threshold at which CD8+ T cell suppression begins in primary human T cells. If supplementation is required, the circuit must use a medium-strength constitutive promoter (PGK or short EF1α) rather than high-output viral promoters, and HO-1 expression levels must be empirically titrated in primary TIF cells before deployment. This remains an open calibration parameter requiring experimental determination.

   116	
   117	### 5.1 Piezoelectric Foundation, Properly Bounded
   118	
   119	Bone is a piezoelectric material. Mechanical deformation generates electrical polarization across the collagen fiber matrix, characterized by Fukada and Yasuda in 1957 and reviewed in subsequent literature [5]. The Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel in osteoblasts and osteocytes transduces mechanical loading into downstream signaling, demonstrating that bone tissue has evolved sophisticated electromechanical transduction machinery [6].
   120	
   121	The architecture's reliance on piezoelectric activity is bounded. Piezoelectric generation is the *primary* power source during active periods when mechanical loading is sufficient. It is not the *sole* power source. The complete energy architecture is specified in §12 and comprises four sources: piezoelectric activity (primary, active), wireless inductive charging (primary, sleep and sedentary), distributed biosynthesized storage (buffer and reserve), and bounded metabolic up-regulation via mitochondrial pathway (reserve, disconnected operation).
   122	
   123	The body uses piezoelectric activity natively as an information-bearing signal (Piezo1 mechanosensation, bone remodeling) rather than as a primary cellular ATP source; bulk cellular ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. The architecture's contribution is to harvest a fraction of the piezoelectric signal for substrate operation while leaving the body's native use of that signal intact.

   126	
   127	The following architecture is proposed on the basis of verified piezoelectric properties of bone. The computational architecture built on this foundation has no direct peer-reviewed precedent and is presented as a novel speculative proposal.
   128	
   129	- **Primary Node: Petrous bone.** Densest bone in the human skull, highest piezoelectric activity, adjacent to cranial nerve pathways. Designated primary processor and neural interface coordinator.
   130

Thoracic vertebrae serve chest cavity organs and sympathetic chain. Lumbar vertebrae serve abdominal organs and bone marrow. Sacral vertebrae serve pelvic organs.

   352	#### 12.3.2 Tissue Safety Constraints
   353	
   354	Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) standards for human exposure to RF fields are established by IEEE C95.1 and ICNIRP guidelines. The IEEE C95.1-1999 standard sets local SAR limits at 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g of tissue; the IEEE C95.1-2005 update revised this to 2 W/kg averaged over 10 g of tissue; the IEEE C95.1-2019 standard refines exposure reference levels and dosimetric reference limits across the relevant frequency range [D5, D6]. Whole-body average SAR limits are 4 W/kg for body exposure and 3.2 W/kg for head exposure under IEC 60601-2-33 [D7]. ICNIRP and FCC guidelines historically derive from the same threshold determination that potentially harmful biological effects occur at whole-body SAR levels of 4 W/kg [D8].
   355	
   356	Direct measurements of RF heating in the presence of metallic medical implants have demonstrated that local SAR can substantially exceed nominal whole-body limits at implant sites — measured local SAR of 24.6 W/kg with associated 4.22 °C temperature elevation in the tail region of artificial hip joints during 1.5T MRI scanning [D7]. This establishes that any WPT architecture involving metallic receiver structures within the body must specifically address local SAR enhancement at the receiver, not only whole-body average SAR.
   357	
   358	For neural-adjacent implants the safety constraint is tighter still. RF-induced heating studies in intracranial electrode arrays demonstrate that head-transmit-receive coils at 2.4 W/kg head-average SAR produce maximum temperature changes below 1 °C at 1.5T but elevated temperatures up to 2 °C at 3T under standard conditions, with substantially higher excursions under fault conditions where lead terminations are electrically shorted [D9].
   359	
   360	#### 12.3.3 Architectural Application
   361	
   362	The wireless charging source deploys receiver coils through the biosynthetic deployment infrastructure of §11. Engineered cells deposit conductive metal (gold, copper, or alloyed metal nanoparticles, sequestered through ferritin-class proteins per §11 refs C11, C14) in coil geometries within the bone substrate, sized to resonate at the carrier frequency of the external charger. Because the coils are biosynthesized from trace dietary inputs and tagged self at formation, they avoid the foreign-body response that conventional implanted coils encounter [§10, §11].
   363	
   364	External charging hardware is conventional: bed surfaces, recliners, and chairs incorporate transmitter coils using standard resonant inductive coupling at sub-MHz frequencies. The choice of operating frequency in the sub-MHz range is deliberate — lower frequencies penetrate tissue with reduced attenuation and produce lower SAR per unit delivered power [D3, D10]. The 6.78 MHz ISM band used in higher-frequency consumer wireless charging is also viable but produces higher local SAR for equivalent delivered power and is reserved for shorter-range high-efficiency applications.
   365	
   366	Receiver placement in the architecture follows a routing constraint motivated by the local-SAR concern: charging coils are placed at sites distant from sensitive neural structures. Pelvic bone, long bones (femur, tibia, humerus), and sternal node receive the primary charging coils. The petrous bone primary node (§5.2) does not host charging coils. Power transmitted through the conductive properties of the skeletal substrate to processing nodes occurs after voltage conditioning and at low currents that do not produce significant local heating.
   367	
   368	#### 12.3.4 MRI Safety Mode
   369	
   370	The wireless charging coils' tunable resonance is exploited as an MRI safety feature. When external strong magnetic fields are detected at any receiver coil, the AI commands all receiver coils to detune to a maximum-impedance state, dramatically reducing local SAR enhancement at the metallic receiver structures. Iron oxide arrays cannot detune but their heating risk is much lower than that of metallic coils. This converts "MRI permanently contraindicated" into "MRI requires detune-mode handshake and cautious imaging parameters," comparable to clinical management for cochlear implants and pacemakers.
   371	
   372	The medical alert protocol for substrate-bearing hosts is specified in §16.
   373	
   374	#### 12.3.5 Switching Logic
   375	
   376	The AI layer monitors substrate energy state through Channel A2 telemetry (mechanical decoding at distributed skeletal nodes per §9.2) and storage levels (capacitive readout, §13). When piezoelectric output drops below a defined threshold and external charging field is detected at receiver coils, the AI switches power management to wireless-primary mode. Piezoelectric output continues to be harvested at whatever rate the residual mechanical loading provides; wireless charging supplements to meet operational demand.
   377	
   378	The AI also schedules computationally intensive operations to wireless-primary periods. Memory consolidation, learning updates, biosynthetic remodeling cycles, and other high-power tasks are deferred to sleep and sedentary periods when the system has access to external power. Active periods run in piezoelectric-primary mode with reduced computational load, prioritizing real-time sensor monitoring and immune-control modulation over deferable processing.
   379	
   380	### 12.4 Source C: Biosynthesized Energy Storage (Buffer and Reserve)
   381	
   382	Storage components are specified in §13 in detail. Brief reference here: storage components draw from any active source (piezoelectric or wireless), retain energy as capacitive charge or chemical state, and discharge to maintain operation during transient mismatches between generation and demand or during periods when no active source is available.
   383	
   384	### 12.5 Source D: Metabolic Up-Regulation via Mitochondrial Pathway (Reserve, Disconnected Operation)
   385	
   386	#### 12.5.1 Mitochondrial Bioenergetics Foundation
   387	
   388	Cellular ATP production in mammalian tissues occurs predominantly through oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, with the electron transport chain (ETC) coupling electron flow from NADH and FADH2 substrates to proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane [E1, E2]. The mammalian ETC comprises complexes I–IV plus the mobile electron carriers ubiquinone and cytochrome c, with electron transfer through the complexes coupled to proton translocation that establishes a transmembrane electrochemical gradient [E1]. The mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) maintained by this gradient drives ATP synthase (Complex V) to produce ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, with optimal ΔΨm range of approximately 80–120 mV for efficient ATP synthesis with minimal reactive oxygen species generation [E3].
   389	
   390	This electron flow is itself an electrical current at cellular scale. The substrate architecture proposed here does not require conversion of ATP to electricity — it requires tapping the electrical activity that is already occurring during ATP production. The proton gradient, the electron flux through the ETC complexes, and the membrane potential are all directly electrical phenomena at the inner mitochondrial membrane.
   391	
   392	#### 12.5.2 Microbial Extracellular Electron Transfer as Architectural Template
   393	
   394	The biological capacity to conduct electrons from intracellular metabolism to extracellular acceptors is established in microbial bioelectrochemistry. *Geobacter* and *Shewanella* species perform extracellular electron transfer (EET) as a metabolic strategy, conducting electrons from internal metabolic processes to external mineral or electrode acceptors through specialized cellular structures [F1, F2]. *Geobacter sulfurreducens* electrically conductive pili (e-pili) are protein filaments that serve as conductive nanowires extending from the cell surface, with characterized genetic basis and structural features [F3, F4]. *Shewanella* species use a combination of outer-membrane c-type cytochromes and conductive nanowires for similar function [F1, F4]. The genes encoding these electron-transfer capabilities have been characterized at sequence and structural level and have been heterologously expressed in other organisms [F1, F4].
   395	
   396	The proposed architectural application is the engineering of cells co-located with mitochondria-rich populations in bone marrow that express microbial EET machinery (or eukaryotic equivalents derived from cytochrome electron transfer chains) to harvest a fraction of mitochondrial electron output during up-regulated activity. The cells do not replace mitochondria; they conduct a small fraction of the surplus electron flow during periods of metabolic up-regulation to the substrate's electrical network.
   397	
   398	This is presented as a proposed mechanism. The constituent biology — mitochondrial electron flow, microbial EET, heterologous expression of EET machinery — is established. The integration of these elements into an AI-directed mitochondrial energy harvesting system in mammalian tissue has no peer-reviewed experimental precedent.

#### 12.3.4 MRI Safety Mode

The wireless charging coils' tunable resonance is exploited as an MRI safety feature. When external strong magnetic fields are detected at any receiver coil, the AI commands all receiver coils to detune to a maximum-impedance state, dramatically reducing local SAR enhancement at the metallic receiver structures. Iron oxide arrays cannot detune but their heating risk is much lower than that of metallic coils. This converts "MRI permanently contraindicated" into "MRI requires detune-mode handshake and cautious imaging parameters," comparable to clinical management for cochlear implants and pacemakers.

The medical alert protocol for substrate-bearing hosts is specified in §16.

#### 12.3.5 Switching Logic

The AI layer monitors substrate energy state through Channel A2 telemetry (mechanical decoding at distributed skeletal nodes per §9.2) and storage levels (capacitive readout, §13). When piezoelectric output drops below a defined threshold and external charging field is detected at receiver coils, the AI switches power management to wireless-primary mode. Piezoelectric output continues to be harvested at whatever rate the residual mechanical loading provides; wireless charging supplements to meet operational demand.

The AI also schedules computationally intensive operations to wireless-primary periods. Memory consolidation, learning updates, biosynthetic remodeling cycles, and other high-power tasks are deferred to sleep and sedentary periods when the system has access to external power. Active periods run in piezoelectric-primary mode with reduced computational load, prioritizing real-time sensor monitoring and immune-control modulation over deferable processing.

### 12.4 Source C: Biosynthesized Energy Storage (Buffer and Reserve)

Storage components are specified in §13 in detail. Brief reference here: storage components draw from any active source (piezoelectric or wireless), retain energy as capacitive charge or chemical state, and discharge to maintain operation during transient mismatches between generation and demand or during periods when no active source is available.

### 12.5 Source D: Metabolic Up-Regulation via Mitochondrial Pathway (Reserve, Disconnected Operation)

#### 12.5.1 Mitochondrial Bioenergetics Foundation

Cellular ATP production in mammalian tissues occurs predominantly through oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria, with the electron transport chain (ETC) coupling electron flow from NADH and FADH2 substrates to proton pumping across the inner mitochondrial membrane [E1, E2]. The mammalian ETC comprises complexes I–IV plus the mobile electron carriers ubiquinone and cytochrome c, with electron transfer through the complexes coupled to proton translocation that establishes a transmembrane electrochemical gradient [E1]. The mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) maintained by this gradient drives ATP synthase (Complex V) to produce ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate, with optimal ΔΨm range of approximately 80–120 mV for efficient ATP synthesis with minimal reactive oxygen species generation [E3].

This electron flow is itself an electrical current at cellular scale. The substrate architecture proposed here does not require conversion of ATP to electricity — it requires tapping the electrical activity that is already occurring during ATP production. The proton gradient, the electron flux through the ETC complexes, and the membrane potential are all directly electrical phenomena at the inner mitochondrial membrane.

#### 12.5.2 Microbial Extracellular Electron Transfer as Architectural Template

The biological capacity to conduct electrons from intracellular metabolism to extracellular acceptors is established in microbial bioelectrochemistry. *Geobacter* and *Shewanella* species perform extracellular electron transfer (EET) as a metabolic strategy, conducting electrons from internal metabolic processes to external mineral or electrode acceptors through specialized cellular structures [F1, F2]. *Geobacter sulfurreducens* electrically conductive pili (e-pili) are protein filaments that serve as conductive nanowires extending from the cell surface, with characterized genetic basis and structural features [F3, F4]. *Shewanella* species use a combination of outer-membrane c-type cytochromes and conductive nanowires for similar function [F1, F4]. The genes encoding these electron-transfer capabilities have been characterized at sequence and structural level and have been heterologously expressed in other organisms [F1, F4].

The proposed architectural application is the engineering of cells co-located with mitochondria-rich populations in bone marrow that express microbial EET machinery (or eukaryotic equivalents derived from cytochrome electron transfer chains) to harvest a fraction of mitochondrial electron output during up-regulated activity. The cells do not replace mitochondria; they conduct a small fraction of the surplus electron flow during periods of metabolic up-regulation to the substrate's electrical network.

This is presented as a proposed mechanism. The constituent biology — mitochondrial electron flow, microbial EET, heterologous expression of EET machinery — is established. The integration of these elements into an AI-directed mitochondrial energy harvesting system in mammalian tissue has no peer-reviewed experimental precedent.
